 Opinion: Idaho should know the real cost of its Medicaid cuts 
 SEN. JIM GUTHRIE
 Oct 29, 2026 
 Oct 29, 2026 
 Updated 
 1 hr ago 
 0 
 Facebook

 Email 
 Sen. Jim Guthrie

 Copy article link 
 Save 
 Earlier this year, I voted against reductions in Idaho's disability services because I believed we needed to ask a question that goes beyond the state budget: What happens to our fellow Idahoans when those services lose funding?
 I am a conservative. I believe government has a responsibility to live within its means, and taxpayers have every right to expect us to spend their money carefully. But caring for people with disabilities should not be reduced to a conservative-versus-liberal argument. It is a human issue, and it is also a question of responsible government.
 Fiscal conservatism requires us to count all the costs of a decision, not just the dollars removed from one budget line. Cutting an appropriation does not necessarily save taxpayers money. Sometimes we simply move the cost somewhere else — to families, hospitals, crisis services, law enforcement, or more expensive forms of care.
 The Legislature reduced state funding for residential habilitation services by approximately $21.8 million. Because Medicaid is jointly funded by the state and federal governments, Idaho also gave up approximately $44 million in associated federal funding. The total reduction was therefore about $65 million, not merely the $21.8 million removed from the state budget.
 Idahoans pay federal taxes whether or not we accept the Medicaid matching funds available to our state for home and community-based services. When we turn down those dollars, our federal tax bills don't go down. The money simply goes elsewhere. Idaho families have contributed to the federal treasury for generations. When their loved ones need disability services, I don't consider leaving available federal funding on the table a fiscal victory.
 We also need to remember who delivers these services.
 We often call these organizations “providers,” but they are also Idaho businesses and employers. They employ thousands of Idahoans in demanding jobs that make it possible for people with disabilities to live in their homes and participate in their communities.
 For several years, I have heard from these service providers that they struggle to pay wages that are competitive with restaurants, retailers, and other employers. When these employers cannot recruit and retain Direct Support Professionals, the consequences extend far beyond their businesses. A person with a disability may lose the support needed to live at home. A parent may have to leave a job to provide care. A family may face a crisis it cannot manage alone.
 Workers can seek better-paying jobs in neighboring states. But families cannot simply move elsewhere to obtain the services their sons and daughters need.
 One provider recently told me that her organization stopped providing an hourly support service because it was losing money on every hour delivered. Before the funding reductions went into effect this year, the organization could at least break even. Eventually, it had to make
 a business decision to preserve the staff and services it could still sustain. That is what a reduction in Medicaid funding may look like on the ground: a service that an Idahoan may need is no longer available from that provider.
 The message I believe we need to hear from these service providers isn't simply, “We need more money.” It is: “We just need enough money.” Enough to hire and retain qualified workers. Enough to provide the services Idaho has authorized. Enough to keep people living successfully in their communities.
 That is why Idaho needs evidence about the impact of these budget reductions.
 Before the 2027 legislative session begins, I believe the Department of Health and Welfare should provide legislators and the public with a clear accounting of what has happened since these reductions took effect. Have providers discontinued services or stopped accepting new participants? Have Direct Support Professional vacancies increased? Are families going without authorized services because workers cannot be found? And in the places where services have disappeared, have costs or responsibilities simply shifted to families or other parts of government?
 Those are questions legislators should have answers to when we consider the next Medicaid budget. But numbers alone won't tell us everything. We also need to hear from Idahoans themselves. Personal stories from people with disabilities, families, workers and service providers can tell us what a spreadsheet cannot: what these decisions mean in people's lives.
 If the reductions can be absorbed without reducing access, destabilizing the workforce or shifting costs elsewhere, the evidence should show us that is what happened. But if Idahoans are losing services, providers are cutting services, families are carrying greater burdens, or costs are simply appearing somewhere else in government or in the health care system, we should be willing to reconsider the decisions we made.
 Fiscal responsibility doesn't end when we pass a budget. It requires us to examine the consequences of our decisions.
 When those consequences adversely affect people with disabilities, their families, and the Idahoans who care for them, we owe them more than an assumption about what may happen when we cut a line on a budget.
 We owe them two things: an honest accounting of the consequences and the courage to change course when the evidence demands it.
 Jim Guthrie is a rancher, business owner, and Republican state senator representing Idaho’s Legislative District 28, which includes Franklin and Power counties and portions of Bannock County in southeastern Idaho.
